nodes.title: Prime-supported positive integers
nodes.statement: For a set P of prime natural numbers, IsPNumber(P,n) means n > 0 and every prime divisor of n belongs to P. The singleton {p} gives exactly the positive powers of p when p is prime; the empty set gives only 1.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Use the natural-number prime divisor predicate, retaining positivity. Prove the product criterion by prime divisibility of a product.
acceptance: The empty prime set admits exactly n=1.
0 is not a P-number, even when P contains every prime.
6 is a {2,3}-number and is not a {3}-number.

sources.match: Defines degree support by a set of primes; positivity excludes a vacuous zero-degree test.

nodes.title: Prime-supported algebraic extensions
nodes.statement: IsPExtension(P,L/K) means L/K is algebraic and every finite intermediate E/K has P-number degree. Neither L/K nor its normal closure is required to be Galois.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Quantify over finite intermediate fields; identify the finite-dimensional case with the single degree [L:K]. Use degree multiplication and finite descent of multiplication tables for towers and filtered unions.
acceptance: K/K is a P-extension.
Q(cuberoot(2))/Q is a {3}-extension, although its normal closure has degree 6.
The two different cubic subfields in the S3 splitting field of X^3−2 are {3}-extensions, while their compositum is not.

nodes.title: Maximal prime-supported extensions
nodes.statement: Inside an algebraic closure every P-extension is contained in a maximal P-extension K_P/K, and K_P is P-closed. If exp.char K = q is prime and q belongs to P, a P-closed K is perfect. Every characteristic-zero field is perfect.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Apply Zorn to P-subextensions; directed unions remain P-extensions. An additional finite P-extension would yield a larger P-extension by transitivity.
In characteristic q, a missing q-th root gives a degree-q purely inseparable extension; in characteristic zero use the perfect-field instance.
acceptance: For P empty the maximal extension is K itself; for P all primes it is the algebraic closure. For P={3}, do not close a chosen cubic extension under normal closure.

sources.match: The maximal P-extension argument uses directed unions and Zorn; perfection follows when the characteristic prime belongs to P.

nodes.title: Linearly disjoint complements
nodes.statement: For algebraic L/M/K in a fixed ambient L, a splitting is an intermediate E/K with E linearly disjoint from M over K and E M = L. Its comparison is the multiplication isomorphism E ⊗_K M ≅ L, with the prescribed two embeddings. Splitting is existence of such an E, without a canonical choice.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Use the existing IntermediateField lattice and linear disjointness. The tensor multiplication is injective by linear disjointness and has image the compositum because the tensor is a field in the algebraic case.
acceptance: The tower M/M/K splits with E=K.
Q(sqrt(2),sqrt(3))/Q(sqrt(2))/Q splits with E=Q(sqrt(3)).
Two distinct cubic subfields in an S3 extension have intersection Q but are not linearly disjoint; their tensor product does not give the degree-6 compositum.

nodes.title: Normalization and valuation prolongations
nodes.statement: For a valuation subring V of K and a finite extension L/K, the integral closure B of V in L is semilocal. Its maximal ideals correspond to the extensions of the valuation ring to L, and B_m is the corresponding valuation ring. More generally every localization A_q of an integrally closed V-subalgebra A ⊆ L is a valuation ring of Frac(A). No finiteness of B as a V-module is asserted.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: For normalization B and a maximal ideal m, apply Aïd Proposition 3.3: normalize a polynomial relation by a coefficient of least valuation and use its successive tail sums. At the first unit coefficient, either x or its inverse belongs to B_m. Proposition 3.6 identifies this localization with any prolongation having centre m.

Proposition 4.1 bounds dim_κ(B/J(B)) by [L:K], by lifting residue-independent elements and normalizing the coefficients of a field-linear relation. This reduced finite-dimensional algebra is a finite product of fields; Theorem 4.4 makes B semilocal and enumerates all prolongations. The maximal-ideal theorem supplies existence; no finite-module normalization is needed.

For an integrally closed V-subalgebra A of L, pass to Frac(A), still finite over K. A contains the integral closure there; localize at q over its contraction and apply ValuationSubring.ofLE to the resulting overring.
acceptance: A finite field extension can have nonfinite normalization over a nondiscrete valuation ring; no finite-module assumption enters the tensor decomposition.

sources.locator: Lemma 2.3.2 proof, pp. 104–105; Lemma 2.3.4 and proof, p. 105
sources.match: Temkin uses normalization and proves the integrally closed subalgebra consequence; the normalization proof is supplied by the public preprint below instead of the unread Bourbaki citation.
Proves the localization/prolongation correspondence and semilocality for a finite extension, using a finite-dimensional reduced residue algebra.

nodes.title: Henselization as a valued field
nodes.statement: For V ⊆ K construct K^h = Frac(V^h), using the imported local-ring henselization. V^h is a valuation ring, K^h/K is separable algebraic and immediate (unchanged residue field and value group), and every compatible embedding into a henselian valued field has a unique extension from K^h. Henselianity of K means exactly HenselianLocalRing(V).
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Use the single pair-henselization carrier reexported by SchemeAndStackFoundations:key/henselization and its ordinary-local comparison. The local HenselianRing instance gives HenselianLocalRing by the simple-root criterion, and the canonical quotient gives the residue-field comparison. Local essentially étale extensions of valuation rings are valuation rings with unchanged value group; pass to the filtered union of pointed étale neighborhoods and take fraction fields.
Identify immediate residue and value-group maps and use the local universal property to obtain the valued-field universal property.
acceptance: For the trivial valuation K^h=K.
For a complete rank-one nonarchimedean field K, K^h=K.
The p-adic henselization of Q is algebraic and immediate over Q and embeds densely in Q_p; it is not Q_p.

sources.match: Uses the immediate separable algebraic henselization of the valued field.
The local étale and henselian constructions preserve the valuation-ring property.

nodes.title: Tensor decomposition by prolongations
nodes.statement: Let L/K be finite, V ⊆ K a valuation ring, and w_1,…,w_r all distinct prolongations to L, counted as valuation rings on the fixed L. Then L ⊗_K K^h ≅ ∏_(i=1)^r L_(w_i)^h as K^h-algebras, with each projection induced by the selected prolongation. This includes inseparable finite extensions.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: The normalization B is semilocal, integral over V, with localizations B_mi the valuation rings. Invoke EGA IV 18.6.8 to identify B ⊗_V V^h with the product of their henselizations.
Invert the nonzero elements of V. The resulting factors are precisely the henselized fraction fields. Integral, rather than finite-module, normalization is enough for the supplier theorem.
acceptance: For a henselian K there is one factor; for a split prime of a number field there are several factors, so the tensor cannot be called a field.

sources.match: The finite field tensor splits into the henselizations at its distinct prolongations, including inseparable extensions.
The ring-level product comparison applies to an integral semilocal algebra over a local ring, without module finiteness.

nodes.title: The valuation-ring étale criterion
nodes.statement: For finite valued L/K, L^h/K^h is unramified exactly when O_L is essentially étale over O_K. Adding equality of residue fields gives the strict version. Étale implies essentially étale always; if the valuation has finite height the two are equivalent. There is no noetherian or rank-one hypothesis in the essentially étale equivalence.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: The essentially étale direction identifies the strict henselizations. In the other direction, descend the finite field generators from a pointed étale neighborhood of O_K^sh.

Intersect the pointed étale domain A′ with L to obtain a Prüfer domain A. The domain A′ is torsion-free and hence flat over A. It is of finite type over A; apply the requested valuation-ring finite-presentation theorem locally on Spec(A). On the open image of Spec(A′)→Spec(A), use EGA IV₄ 17.7.5(iv) to descend finite presentation and 17.7.7 to descend étaleness at the selected point. The selected localization of A is O_L. This source-side descent is distinct from the pinned scalar-extension descent theorem.
At finite height Spec(O_K) has finitely many points; an étale algebra has finite fibres, so the relevant localization is obtained by one inversion and remains étale.
acceptance: The definition of unramified used here is the henselized one specified in GF.2. Strictly essentially étale means equal residue fields, not separably closed residue fields.

sources.match: Proves the essentially étale equivalence without a height bound and the étale equivalence at finite height.

Finite presentation descends along a faithfully flat morphism locally of finite presentation, with the stated quasi-compactness or quasi-separatedness condition; for locally finitely presented source and target, étaleness of the composite descends at a point where the intermediate map is flat.
A flat finite-type algebra over an arbitrary valuation ring is finitely presented; applying this at valuation localizations supplies the Prüfer step.

nodes.title: The ramification tower
nodes.statement: Fix a prolongation of V to K^a and the embedded separable closure K^s. Define K^h ⊆ K^u ⊆ K^t ⊆ K^s, where K^u is the maximal unramified extension of K^h and K^t its maximal tame extension. The integer ring of K^u is V^sh. In Gal(K^s/K), use the existing ValuationSubring.decompositionSubgroup for D and its existing inertiaSubgroup for I; view I in G_K through its subgroup inclusion. Prove that D fixes K^h and I fixes K^u, and use the H1 wild subgroup W to identify its fixed field with K^t. D/I ≅ Gal(κ^s/κ). D and I may be proper subgroups; K^h/K need not be normal, so no quotient by D is used.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Use the imported strict-localization theorem to realize K^u and the decomposition/inertia correspondence. Over K^u apply the strictly henselian arbitrary-rank tame theorem to form K^t.
Translate closed subgroups and fixed fields by infinite Galois theory. The Kummer pairing describes Gal(K^t/K^u) using the prime-to-p divisible hull of Γ_K and all prime-to-p roots of unity in K^u.

For prime p use the pinned IsProPSylow carrier and its existence, conjugacy and normal uniqueness results to compare the supplied wild subgroup and to transport it under a change of prolongation. For p=1 use W=1 directly.
acceptance: For henselian K, K^h=K and D is the whole Galois group.
For trivial V, K^u=K^t=K^s and I=W=1.
If exp.char κ=1 then K^t=K^s and W=1.
The p-adic henselization of Q need not be normal over Q; treat D as a subgroup, not a quotient.
For trivially valued F_p(t), W=1 and (K^s)^W=K^s, whereas (K^a)^W=K^a is strictly larger. The fixed-field comparison must name its ambient separable closure.

nodes.title: Tame algebraic extensions
nodes.statement: A selected valued algebraic L/K is tame when L^h/K^h is tame. For finite henselian L/K, let M/K be its maximal unramified subextension; tameness means [L:M] is prime to p=exp.char κ_K. Equivalently κ_L/κ_K is separable, Γ_L/Γ_K has order prime to p, and [L:K]=[κ_L:κ_K]·[Γ_L:Γ_K]. For arbitrary algebraic extensions require this at every finite henselian level. The equality retains finiteness and excludes defect.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Use the prime-to-p tame tower over K^u supplied by H1. Descend to finite henselian subextensions using their maximal unramified part.

The finite degree formula follows from the Kummer pairing over K^u and the residue classification. It must not be imposed on the degree [L:K] of a nonhenselian extension, where multiple prolongations change that degree.

nodes.title: Tower and filtered-union laws
nodes.statement: For each of the six properties strictly unramified, unramified, tame, henselian extension, totally ramified and purely wild, an algebraic tower M/L/K has the property exactly when both steps do. Each property is preserved under directed unions of subextensions. For a selected prolongation, L^h=LK^h, L^u=LK^u and L^t=LK^t inside a common valued algebraic closure. Unramified and tame extensions are preserved by every valued base change and every selected prolongation on the compositum.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: The first three properties are membership in their maximal closure. For the disjointness properties use the displayed compositum identities and tensor associativity.
All finite linear-independence relations occur at finite levels; commute local henselization with filtered colimits for the union statement.

For an arbitrary compatible valued base change the residue characteristic is unchanged. A pointed essentially étale algebra remains essentially étale. For tame extensions, pass to the strict henselizations and use their prime-to-p radical description; base change preserves that description. This proves the two base-change laws without asserting degree preservation for arbitrary base changes.
acceptance: Check each of the six properties separately on identity towers. The compositum formulas must use the chosen prolongations and preserve the two multiplication maps.

sources.match: Proves transitivity in both directions and stability under filtered unions for the six extension classes, together with the closure-compositum formulas.

The arbitrary-rank character pairing restricts to the existing tame inertia character with its arithmetic Frobenius action x↦x^q.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: A local field is henselian, its residue field is perfect, and its finite extensions satisfy [L:K]=ef. Substitute these three supplied facts into the henselian criteria.
Compare the action on uniformizer roots with the existing tame character. Keep the arithmetic Frobenius convention from the supplier rather than choosing an opposite generator.

nodes.title: The tame tower under perfection
nodes.statement: Let K have characteristic q>0 and let K^perf be its perfection with the unique prolonged valuation. The canonical equivalence of separable extensions identifies L/K with L K^perf/K^perf, preserves degrees, and preserves unramified and tame extensions after the corresponding henselizations. In a common algebraic closure (K^perf)^t=K^t K^perf. The residue fields and value groups change by purely inseparable extension and q-divisible hull, respectively. In characteristic zero the comparison is the identity. For every prime set P, K is separably P-closed if and only if K^perf is P-closed.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Use separable/purely-inseparable linear disjointness and Frobenius descent of a finite separable polynomial to identify finite separable extensions and their degrees. Unique valuation prolongation across purely inseparable fields gives the valued correspondence.

Henselization commutes with the purely inseparable base change after taking the corresponding fraction fields. Separable residue extensions descend uniquely, and the prime-to-q part of the value quotient is unaffected by adjoining q-power roots. The strict henselian inertia pairing therefore identifies the tame towers. This is a statement about the separable tame theory, not that all algebraic extensions of an imperfect K become tame.

A finite separable extension of K^perf descends to a finite purely inseparable level. Apply a sufficiently high Frobenius power to its defining polynomial to descend to K with the same degree; conversely use separable/purely-inseparable disjointness. Since K^perf is perfect, this proves the closedness equivalence for each P.
acceptance: For F_p(t) with its t-adic valuation the perfection changes Z to Z[1/p]. A prime-to-p radical remains tame of the same degree; an Artin–Schreier extension with pole order one must not be declared tame after perfection.

sources.locator: §2.4.6, p. 108; proof of Theorem 2.5.5, p. 110; derived comparison for the separable repair E6
sources.match: The proof passes through perfection in the splitting argument; the stated comparison expands the required separable/tame invariance using disjointness and the residue/value descriptions.

hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Order the admissible intermediate fields by inclusion. The GF.2 directed-union theorem supplies upper bounds for chains; apply Zorn in the fixed algebraic closure. Repeat in the separable closure.
acceptance: With S empty, the maximal object is the algebraic closure.
With S={tame}, the maximal object is K^t.
For Q_p a maximal purely wild extension cannot contain a nontrivial tame radical of prime-to-p degree.

nodes.title: Unramified and tame complements
nodes.statement: If K_hu/K is maximal among extensions that are both henselian extensions and unramified, then K^h ⊗_K K_hu ≅ K^u. If K_rt/K is maximal among tame totally ramified extensions, then K^u ⊗_K K_rt ≅ K^t. Both maps are multiplication maps with the chosen factor embeddings.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: The disjointness halves follow from the definitions. For the first compositum equality, maximality forces the residue field of K_hu to be separably closed: otherwise lift a finite separable residue extension to a further henselian unramified extension.
For the second equality compare residue fields and value groups. If Γ_(K_rt) is smaller than the prime-to-p divisible hull, adjoin a missing prime-to-p root and contradict maximality.
acceptance: With trivial valuation the first complement is K^s and the second is K. In each case check tensor injectivity as well as the compositum equality.

sources.match: Constructs the first two complement pairs by maximality, separably closed residue and prime-to-p divisibility of the value group.

nodes.title: Field-theoretic splitting equivalences
nodes.statement: For a class C of valued fields closed under algebraic extensions, the following assertions, each quantified over K in C, are equivalent: some maximal purely wild K_w splits K^a/K^t/K; every maximal purely wild K_w does; every maximal purely wild K_w is a tame field; and K is tame exactly when it has no nontrivial purely wild extension. There are corresponding separable assertions, replacing K^a by K^s and tame by separably tame. Over henselian K only, the splitting is equivalent to a continuous section Gal(K^t/K)→G_K of the quotient map G_K→Gal(K^t/K). For nonhenselian K use a closed complement to W as a subgroup factorization, without assuming W normal in G_K.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Every complement implies existence of one. Existence for K with no nontrivial purely wild extension forces that complement to be K, hence K^a=K^t. Conversely a tame field has no nontrivial purely wild extension.

Apply that characterization to a maximal purely wild K_w, which admits no further purely wild extension. If K_w is tame, then K^a/(K^t K_w) is both tame and purely wild, hence trivial. The same argument inside K^s gives the separable version.

For henselian fields use the Galois correspondence and perfection to translate the splitting to a continuous section. In the nonhenselian case K^t/K can fail to be normal; the printed semidirect-product formulation needs this correction.
acceptance: For Q with its 2-adic valuation, the S3 splitting field of X^3−X−2 has wild inertia of order 2. This subgroup is not normal in S3, ruling out a general quotient by wild inertia.

nodes.title: Pank splitting over a henselian field
nodes.statement: Let K be henselian with arbitrary-rank valuation and residual characteristic exponent p. Every maximal purely wild K_w/K gives a multiplication isomorphism K^t ⊗_K K_w ≅ K^a. The separable version gives K^t ⊗_K K_sw ≅ K^s for every maximal separable purely wild K_sw. For p=1 these statements reduce to K^t=K^s and K_w=K^perf.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: For prime p, G1 gives cd_p(G_(κ_K))≤1. A p-Sylow S of G_K/W maps onto a p-Sylow T of G_(κ_K); its kernel lies in the prime-to-p group I/W and is trivial, so S≅T. The existing Sylow comparison of ordinary cohomological dimension gives cd_p(G_K/W)=cd_p(S)=cd_p(T)=cd_p(G_(κ_K))≤1. No finite-generation hypothesis or free-pro-p criterion is needed.

Use the general pro-p-kernel lifting theorem on G_K→G_K/W and on the closed subgroup corresponding to any given purely wild subextension. The section yields a complement containing that subextension on the field side, giving the result for every maximal choice.
Pass between the separable and full algebraic closures through perfection, which preserves the tame tower. The p=1 case is separate and uses no pro-1 Sylow terminology.
acceptance: A Schur–Zassenhaus argument alone is insufficient when the residue absolute Galois group has p-quotients. The two additional supplier inputs are listed as gaps and a proposed Profinite Cohomology Part II.

nodes.title: Rank-one norm and root-continuity bridge
nodes.statement: For a nontrivially valued height-one K, choose an order embedding of its actual value group into positive reals and the associated ultrametric norm. Its completion is henselian, contains K^h, and K is dense in K^h. In a normal algebraic extension of a henselian rank-one normed field the Krasner inequality gives x∈K(y), with x separable, y algebraic, and |x−y| strictly smaller than every distance from x to a distinct conjugate. Roots of a monic separable polynomial vary continuously with its coefficients; sufficiently close monic polynomials of the same degree have their roots uniquely paired beyond the largest conjugate-closeness bound.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Embed the archimedean ordered value group in the reals, transfer the norm and use Newton approximation in the complete ultrametric field to obtain Hensel lifting. The henselization universal property embeds K^h in the completion, proving density.

Extend the rank-one norm to a normal algebraic closure of the henselian field. Uniqueness of valuation prolongations makes all automorphisms isometries. The usual conjugate-separation argument proves the IsKrasner interface even without completeness of the base; the pinned complete-space theorem alone does not provide this generality.

For root continuity evaluate f−g at each root, bound its value by the coefficient minimum, and factor the other polynomial into linear terms. If no root were close, the sum of the factor values would contradict that bound. Theorems 14 and 16 give a non-strict root-distance bound at a threshold chosen strictly beyond all conjugate distances; separability and disjoint balls then give uniqueness. To require a strict root-distance bound at a prescribed threshold, first enlarge that threshold.
acceptance: Strict inequalities are required: for f=(X−1)(X+1) over Q with the 2-adic valuation, taking the conjugate-closeness bound itself does not distinguish the two roots.

nodes.title: Descent from the henselization
nodes.statement: If K has height one and L/K^h is separable algebraic, there is an algebraic henselian extension E/K and a compatible valued isomorphism E^h ≅ L with E ⊗_K K^h ≅ L. For finite L/K^h choose E/K finite of the same degree. No claim is made for inseparable L/K^h or arbitrary height.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: At finite degree choose a primitive element of L/K^h and its monic separable minimal polynomial f. Approximate its coefficients by those of g∈K[X]. Root continuity and Krasner give K^h(beta)=L; degree equality forces g irreducible over both K and K^h. Put E=K(beta). Its tensor with K^h is L, so it has unique prolongation.

For an infinite separable extension use maximal compatible pairs (E, E^h↪L) under extension. A chain has an upper bound by filtered compatibility. If E^h is not all L, apply the finite argument over E to a proper finite subextension of L/E^h, contradicting maximality. Arbitrary unrelated finite descents cannot simply be unioned.
acceptance: For L=K^h one may take E=K. At finite degree require [E:K]=[L:K^h]. In the infinite case verify compatibility of the chosen embeddings along every chain.

nodes.title: Maximal separable wildness under henselization
nodes.statement: If K has height one, then E/K is a maximal separable purely wild extension exactly when E/K is a henselian extension and E^h/K^h is maximal separable purely wild.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: A further separable purely wild extension above E remains such after henselization. Conversely descend a finite nontrivial separable purely wild extension above E^h using decompletion over E, and use the henselian-disjointness comparison to retain its degree and pure wildness.
acceptance: Verify the extension E/K has unique prolongation in the reverse implication. Henselization alone must not turn an arbitrary non-purely-wild E/K into a maximal purely wild extension.

nodes.title: Pank splitting in height one
nodes.statement: If K has height one, without a henselian hypothesis, every maximal purely wild K_w satisfies K^t ⊗_K K_w ≅ K^a. Every maximal separable purely wild K_sw satisfies K^t ⊗_K K_sw ≅ K^s.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: If K is perfect, so is K_w. The preceding comparison makes K_w K^h maximal purely wild over K^h, and henselian Pank plus tensor associativity gives the splitting.

For imperfect K pass to its perfection, apply the perfect case and the tame-tower comparison, and obtain one complement over K. The corrected field-theoretic splitting equivalences promote existence to every maximal choice.

nodes.title: Tameness in height one
nodes.statement: If K has height one, residual characteristic exponent p, and is p-closed (with p=1 meaning the empty prime set), then K is tame.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: A maximal purely wild extension is a p-extension; p-closedness makes it trivial. Height-one Pank then gives K^t=K^a.
acceptance: Every residue-characteristic-zero height-one field satisfies the empty-prime closedness hypothesis. Q_p fails the prime-p hypothesis because X^p−p gives a nontrivial p-extension.

nodes.title: Composition by a residue valuation
nodes.statement: Let V be a valuation subring of K and R a valuation subring of κ_V. Define V∘R as the inverse image of R under V→κ_V, viewed as a subring of K. It is a valuation ring. Conversely, if U⊆V are valuation subrings of K, U is this pullback of the induced valuation ring on κ_V, and V=U_P for P=U∩m_V. Use the existing ofPrime/idealOfLE inverse laws to identify coarsenings; do not construct a second localization API.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: For x outside V its inverse lies in the maximal ideal of V and thus in the pullback. For a unit of V, use the valuation-ring alternative for its residue. This proves the valuation-ring axiom for the inverse image.
For a coarsening V of U, reduce U in κ_V and use the localization inverse laws at P. The associated ordered groups fit into 0→Γ_R→Γ_U→Γ_V→0 with convex kernel, and the final residue field is κ_R.
acceptance: Taking the trivial valuation on κ_V recovers V.
Compose the t-adic valuation on Q_p((t)) with the p-adic valuation on Q_p. The resulting valuation has lexicographic value group Z×Z, with v(t)=(1,0), v(p)=(0,1).

nodes.statement: Use ringKrullDim(V) as valuation height, without defining a second dimension invariant. If this dimension equals a natural d, construct the ordered chain of the d+1 prime ideals of V. For every 0≤i≤d construct the unique coarsening K_i of height i, and the induced valued residue field κ_i of height d−i. Identify height with the convex-subgroup rank of the ordered value group. Height zero means the trivial valuation.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Use prime ideals/convex subgroups and their reverse-order coarsening correspondence. For finite height, a chain of dimension d has exactly d+1 primes; localize at the unique prime producing height i.

nodes.title: Abhyankar inequality and the height bound
nodes.statement: For a valued field extension L/K of finite transcendence degree, rr(Γ_L/Γ_K)+trdeg(κ_L/κ_K) ≤ trdeg(L/K), where rr(A)=dim_Q(A⊗_Z Q). For every ordered abelian group of finite rational rank, its convex-subgroup rank is at most that rational rank. Consequently a field of finite transcendence degree over its prime field, and every algebraic extension of it, has finite valuation height. The general inequality is owned here; no analytic topological-transcendence-degree equality is asserted.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Choose finitely many elements with rationally independent values modulo Γ_K and units with algebraically independent residues over κ_K. In any polynomial relation, collect monomials by value. Rational independence separates value blocks, and residue independence prevents cancellation in a block of least value. Thus all chosen elements are algebraically independent.

In a strict finite chain of convex subgroups select one element per successive difference. They are rationally independent: the summand in the highest convex layer cannot be canceled by lower layers. Hence height≤rational rank.

A valuation on Q has rank at most one (the p-adic or trivial restriction), and on a finite prime field is trivial. Apply the inequality to finite-transcendence-degree extensions; an algebraic extension has torsion value quotient and algebraic residue extension, so the bound persists.
acceptance: For K=F_p(t) with t-adic valuation, rational rank 1 plus residue transcendence degree 0 equals trdeg(K/F_p)=1. For a Gauss valuation with t of value 0 the two contributions are 0 and 1 instead.

sources.locator: Kuhlmann–Kuhlmann–Visan, §2 Lemma 2.1, author pp. 6–7, and formula (12), p. 8; Temkin Theorem 2.6.6 proof, p. 112
sources.match: The independence argument bounds rational rank plus residue transcendence degree. The convex-chain argument in this node then gives the finite-height consequence needed by Temkin.

nodes.title: Unramifiedness under composition
nodes.statement: Let L/K be algebraic, K of finite height d, and 0≤i≤d. Then L/K is unramified exactly when both L_i/K_i and κ_(L_i)/κ_(K_i), with their induced residual valuations, are unramified.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Reduce to finite extensions by the tower/union laws. From an étale valuation-ring map, localize for the coarse extension and quotient for the residual extension; radical equality follows because the étale quotient is reduced.

For the converse use Temkin 2010 Proposition 2.2.2. The composed ring map is torsion-free hence flat; the coarse and residual maximal-ideal equations imply the composed one. At finite height invert one element to obtain the coarsening. Scale coarse generators into the fine ring and add residue generators to obtain finite type. For finite presentation apply the imported flattening-by-blowup theorem over Spec(V), with the generic point as the quasi-compact open: that point is open at finite height and the generic algebra is a finite separable field. Every finitely generated nonzero ideal of a valuation ring is principal, so the admissible blowup is an isomorphism, and its strict transform is the original flat algebra. The imported theorem therefore supplies finite presentation. Flatness, finite presentation and the separable residual fibre give étaleness.
acceptance: For the composite valuation on Q_p((t)), an unramified constant extension gives both required unramified steps. The extension s^ell=t, ell>1, fails at the coarse step.

sources.locator: Lemma 2.6.3(i) and proof, p. 111; Temkin 2010 Proposition 2.2.2 and proof, author pp. 11–12
sources.match: Proves unramifiedness of a composed extension from the coarse and residual conditions; the auxiliary finite-presentation input is imported from general flattening.
Alternative public proof of the valuation-ring finite-type/flat to finite-presentation implication; the general flattening theorem is imported from its owner.
Provides the composed-ring generation and maximal-ideal argument.

nodes.title: Tameness under composition
nodes.statement: Under the preceding finite-height hypotheses let p=exp.char κ_K be the FINAL residue exponent and p_i=exp.char κ_(K_i) the coarse residue exponent. Then L/K is tame exactly when L_i/K_i and the residual valued extension are tame and Γ_(L_i)/Γ_(K_i) has no nonzero p-torsion. The torsion condition is automatic if p_i=p. For p=1 it is vacuous.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Reduce to finite subextensions and pass compatibly to the maximal unramified extensions using the preceding composition result.
Over a strictly henselian field, a tame finite extension is generated by prime-to-p radicals. Their coarse and residual extensions are tame, with no coarse p-torsion.

Conversely, if the finite extension over the strict henselization is not tame, its degree is divisible by p. If the coarse extension is tame, its degree is the product of its coarse e and f. Either coarse e has a p-factor or the residual degree has one, which prevents residual tameness. Here p is the residual exponent of the induced residual valuation, not necessarily the characteristic of the coarse residue field.
acceptance: Take K=Q_p((t)) with the t-adic/p-adic composite valuation and L=Q_p((s)), s^p=t. The coarse extension is tame in residue characteristic zero and the residual extension is the identity on Q_p; the coarse value quotient Z/p violates the extra condition, and the full extension is wild.

sources.locator: Lemma 2.6.3(ii) and proof, pp. 111–112, with source issue E4 corrected
sources.match: Adds the absence of final-residue-prime torsion in the coarse value quotient to the two tame conditions; the final prime corrects the printed proof.

nodes.title: Tame fields under composition
nodes.statement: For finite-height K and K_i as above, K is tame exactly when K_i and its residually valued κ_i are tame fields and Γ_(K_i) is p-divisible, with p the final residue exponent. If p_i=p, divisibility follows from tameness of K_i and need not be assumed separately.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Apply tame composition to K^a/K. Its coarse field is an algebraic closure of K_i and its residue is an algebraic closure of κ_i.

The absence of p-torsion in the algebraically closed value-group quotient is equivalent to p-divisibility of the original coarse group. If K_i is tame with residual exponent p, its algebraic radical extensions already give this divisibility.
acceptance: The coarse t-adic field Q_p((t)) is tame in residue characteristic zero, but the composed field cannot be declared tame: its coarse value group Z is not p-divisible and its residual valued Q_p is not tame.

sources.match: Applies the preceding extension criterion to an algebraic closure; the torsion condition becomes p-divisibility of the coarse value group.

nodes.title: Residues and values of a p-closed field
nodes.statement: Let K be p-closed, p prime, with final residue characteristic p. For every coarsening V_i, the field κ_i is p-closed as an abstract field, and Γ_(K_i) is p-divisible. If exp.char κ_i=1, use characteristic-zero-residue tameness for the coarse field, not an induction hypothesis with the wrong residue prime.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: Every element of K has a p-th root: if X^p−a had no root it would be irreducible for prime p (the binomial irreducibility criterion), giving a forbidden degree-p extension. Thus each coarsened value group is p-divisible. If a coarse residue field has characteristic p, lifting an element to a unit and taking such a root proves that residue field perfect.

A finite p-extension of a coarse residue field is therefore separable: the residue field is either of characteristic zero or perfect of characteristic p. Choose its primitive monic irreducible polynomial and lift its coefficients to the coarse valuation ring. A factorization upstairs would have monic integral factors, whose reductions contradict residual irreducibility. Its degree is a p-power, so it defines a forbidden nontrivial finite p-extension of K.
acceptance: Include the trivial coarsening, whose residue is K itself. For a nontrivial coarsening, identify the final residue prime separately from the characteristic of its intermediate residue field.

sources.match: The finite-height proof uses p-closedness of the coarsened residue fields and p-divisibility of coarsened values; this node supplies the lifting arguments.

nodes.title: Tameness at finite height
nodes.statement: Every finite-height valued field K of residual characteristic exponent p that is p-closed is tame.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: At height zero, p-closedness gives perfection when needed and the trivial valuation is tame on a perfect field. Height one is GF.4.

At height d>1 choose 0<i<d. The coarsening and its residually valued residue field have smaller heights. Their fields are p-closed; apply induction when their residual exponent is p, and use automatic tameness when the coarse residue characteristic is zero.
Use p-divisibility of the coarse value group and the tame-field composition criterion.
acceptance: Verify height zero through perfection, height one through the Pank corollary, and a height-two mixed-characteristic example through the extra coarse p-divisibility condition.

sources.match: Inducts on finite valuation height using height-one tameness and the composed-valuation criterion.

nodes.title: Finite-height descent inside a p-closed field
nodes.statement: Let K be a p-closed valued field with final residue exponent p, and L/K finite. There is a subfield K_0⊆K, relatively algebraically closed in K, of finite transcendence degree over the prime field, and a finite L_0/K_0 such that multiplication gives L_0⊗_(K_0)K ≅ L with the selected valuation. K_0 is p-closed and has finite height. Although K_0 need not be finitely generated after taking relative algebraic closure, its transcendence degree and valuation-height bound remain finite.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: K is perfect. A finite primitive polynomial for L/K uses finitely many coefficients; adjoin these to the prime field and then take the relative algebraic closure K_0 in K. K_0 is perfect because any purely inseparable root in perfect K is algebraic over K_0.

The extension K/K_0 is regular: a relatively algebraically closed perfect subfield is linearly disjoint from every finite algebraic extension. One proof passes to a finite normal closure and uses the Galois correspondence; the purely inseparable part is trivial over perfect K_0. Thus the polynomial still defines L_0 and its multiplication tensor is L.
If K_0 had a nontrivial finite p-extension E, regular disjointness would make EK/K a p-extension of the same degree, contradicting p-closedness. Apply the Abhyankar/height bound to K_0.
acceptance: Include every coefficient of the primitive polynomial before taking relative algebraic closure. Verify regular disjointness preserves its degree; do not assert the relatively closed subfield is finitely generated.

sources.match: Descends a finite extension to the relative algebraic closure of a field generated by finitely many coefficients; finite transcendence degree, not finite generation, gives finite height.

nodes.title: Tameness of p-closed valued fields
nodes.statement: Let K be a field with any Krull valuation, including a valuation of infinite height, and let p be its residue characteristic exponent. If K has no nontrivial finite p-extension, then every algebraic valued extension of K is tame: K^a=K^t. When p=1, p-extension means a degree-1 extension, and the conclusion holds for every valued field of residue characteristic zero.
hypotheses: All field maps and valuations are compatible as fixed in the conventions; algebraic closures carry the chosen prolongation.
proofSteps: For each finite L/K descend the selected valuation and its field extension to L_0/K_0 as above. Finite-height tameness makes L_0/K_0 tame; stability of tame extensions under arbitrary valued base change makes L/K tame.
Every finite subextension is tame, so the full algebraic closure is tame by the directed-union law. No completeness, perfect residue field, discreteness or henselian hypothesis is used.
acceptance: With trivial valuation the conclusion reduces to perfection. At residue exponent 1 the hypothesis is automatic. A field such as Q_p must fail the p-closed hypothesis rather than contradict the conclusion.

nodes.title: The separable prime-supported tameness export
nodes.statement: For a prime set P, if K has no nontrivial finite separable P-extension, then every finite separable L/K is tame for every prolongation whose final residue characteristic p belongs to P. At residue characteristic zero the same conclusion is automatic. For fully P-closed K the corresponding assertion holds for all algebraic extensions. These are respectively separable P-tameness and P-tameness; neither asserts tameness at residue primes outside P.

For a valuation with residual prime p∈P, the perfection is p-closed. Apply general tameness there, then descend tameness of finite separable L/K through the perfection comparison. For fully P-closed K apply the p-closed theorem directly.
